strengths: The paper proposes a useful, conceptually simple combination of graph-based semi-supervised learning and classifier-based Bayesian optimization. Exploiting the geometry of unevaluated candidates is particularly well motivated for fixed candidate pools.

The empirical evaluation includes GP-based methods and several BORE/LFBO classifiers across synthetic functions, tabular hyperparameter optimization, NATS-Bench, and an image-based task. Twenty repetitions with standard errors provide meaningful evidence, with particularly promising results on NATS-Bench.

The paper provides pseudocode, benchmark search spaces, and substantial sensitivity studies covering bandwidth, unlabeled sample count, sampling distribution, pool subsampling, and threshold ratio. It also acknowledges that existing semi-supervised learning bounds do not directly apply to adaptive optimization.
weaknesses: The principal contribution is not adequately isolated. Figure 12 includes a valuable labeled-only kernel baseline, but it sometimes outperforms the variants using unlabeled data, notably on Bukin6 and Branin with label spreading. This ablation fixes beta at 0.5, whereas the main comparisons learn beta. A competitive labeled-only baseline with controlled bandwidth and acquisition tie-breaking is needed to establish whether the gains arise from unlabeled data rather than the different surrogate or optimization heuristic.

The explanation for improved exploration is insufficiently supported. Sampling truncated Gaussians around evaluated points does not ensure Assumption 4.1: high-density paths can cross objective-threshold class boundaries. Appendix C asserts that unlabeled points reduce the margin and expand the favorable decision region without establishing either implication. Its cited classification bounds are explicitly inapplicable to this sequential setting. The visual examples and regret curves demonstrate possible benefits, but do not directly establish the claimed exploration mechanism.

Important implementation details remain unclear. The paper describes continuous L-BFGS-B acquisition maximization without explaining candidate selection for discrete fixed pools. Input scaling, label-spreading alpha, propagation stopping settings, and beta optimization bounds and initialization are also unspecified. These choices materially affect graph connectivity and reproducibility, especially across heterogeneous tabular variables and image embeddings.

The evidence for broader applicability is limited. All continuous benchmarks are two-dimensional. The 64-dimensional MNIST experiment uses embeddings trained on 440,000 images to predict the exact three-digit objective class. Although the training and test images are separated, this supplies substantial objective-specific supervision and favorable representation geometry. A baseline selecting candidates using the pretrained classifier would help establish the usefulness of optimization in this setting.

Computational tradeoffs are incompletely evaluated. Dense graph construction, repeated propagation, bandwidth optimization, and 1,000 acquisition restarts can introduce substantial overhead. The timing study varies pool size with fixed beta on synthetic problems; it does not report comparative runtime or the cost of adaptive bandwidth fitting used in the main experiments.

A smaller mathematical presentation issue should be corrected: the column-normalized definition of p_ij implies P = W D^{-1}, whereas the text states P = D^{-1} W. Because Equation 11 subsequently transposes P, this inconsistency leaves the implemented propagation rule ambiguous.
